meta_description: How Dataq Software engineers pharmaceuticals and biotech: trial eligibility and recruitment intelligence, risk-based monitoring, pharmacovigilance intake and signal detection, submission-grade RWE pipelines, manufacturing data spines and CSA validation acceleration under GxP duty.

blocks.x: In pharmaceutical and biotech operations, the costly middle of the pipeline is made of waiting: cohorts that wait on chart review, monitoring visits that wait on schedules, adverse-event cases that wait on manual assembly, batches that wait on paperwork, evidence that waits on a rebuild for every new study. The science is fast; the information plumbing around it is not — and the plumbing carries a regulator. GCP, GVP and GMP duties, ALCOA+ data integrity, eCTD conventions and inspection readiness mean every acceleration has to arrive with its audit story attached. This page is the engineering picture of that machinery as Dataq Software sees it from inside R&D, safety and manufacturing estates — where it leaks months, and the six deep builds that recover them.
How the pipeline runs, assay to approval

The upstream starts with data that no warehouse was designed for: high-throughput screening plates, high-content imaging runs, assay results from instruments whose formats change with the vendor generation. Results land in LIMS and ELN systems under GxP data-integrity duties; hit triage and candidate selection run on analysis pipelines that must be reproducible because a regulator may one day ask how a decision was made. When a candidate advances, the chemistry and manufacturing story — CMC — becomes its own documentation burden, and tech transfer to a site replays every method, every validation, every deviation history in a new context.

Clinical development industrializes the protocol. EDC forms capture the visit data, ePRO and eCOA devices capture the patient's day, IRT randomizes and supplies the trial, CTMS schedules the sites, and risk-based monitoring decides where monitors travel and what they verify against source. Every protocol deviation accumulates with its own clock. Safety intake runs continuously: adverse events arrive from sites, literature, registries and call centers in dozens of languages, get coded into MedDRA, assemble into E2B cases, and clock against GVP reporting deadlines while signal detection watches the cumulative database.

At the end of the funnel, everything converges on the submission: analysis-ready datasets to CDISC standards, CSRs, and an eCTD dossier assembled across submissions-ready content. Manufacturing runs in parallel under GMP: MES executes the batch, LIMS releases the results, the eQMS accumulates deviations and CAPA, serialization and cold-chain systems track every unit for DSCSA and FMD compliance, and batch release waits on a disposition that is only as fast as the paperwork underneath it. Real-world evidence — claims and EHR-derived data — extends the story post-approval, under provenance rules the submission team will enforce.
The estate underneath: systems this work touches

Pharma programs succeed or fail on how honestly the estate is mapped before anything is built. Dataq Software starts every engagement by naming the systems, their owners, their validation status and their data contracts. The table below is the estate we most often find and integrate against in R&D, clinical, safety and manufacturing programs — not a generic stack diagram.

blocks.x: Where the pipeline leaks months

Ask R&D, clinical operations and quality leaders where the time goes and the answers converge on the same eight places. Dataq Software's diagnostic scores each of them in your own estate before recommending a build, because the leak that dominates a mid-cap biotech is often different from the one that dominates a big-pharma portfolio — and the fix is engineering either way.

items: Screening pipelines that compute before they think

Assay and screening pipelines run compute-bound workloads on estates sized by habit, while reproducibility — the thing validation actually requires — is bolted on by documentation. HPC and GPU capacity sits idle in the windows between campaigns. The measurable waste is wall-clock per campaign and the rerun rate when an environment cannot be reproduced.
Eligibility matching stuck at chart review

Protocol criteria live as PDFs while the patients live in EHR data; coordinators screen by hand and the trial misses its enrollment window. Site telemetry shows the conversion gap, but nobody can compute the population the protocol actually describes. This is a query-engineering problem wearing a recruitment costume.
Monitoring travel that misses the risk

Risk-based monitoring exists as a policy, but KRIs are computed in spreadsheets monthly, so monitors travel to the sites the schedule expected rather than the ones the data now flags. Deviations are found after the visit. SDV hours stay high while the risks that matter — enrollment drift, data-entry lag, protocol confusion — accumulate unwatched.
PV intake breaching reporting clocks

Adverse events arrive from sites, literature, call centers and partners in dozens of languages; case assembly is manual, MedDRA coding is bottlenecked on reviewers, and reporting clocks get worked at the wire. The backlog is measurable in days-per-case and in the percentage of cases worked inside their final reporting window.
RWE rebuilt per study, provenance thin

Every real-world evidence request re-derives its cohorts from raw claims and EHR extracts, with lineage documented in emails. When the evidence has to survive submission scrutiny or a payer dossier review, the provenance gap becomes the project. Assembly time is measured in months for work that is fundamentally a query over governed data.
Batch release queuing behind paperwork

MES executes the batch, LIMS releases the results, but the disposition packet assembles by hand across eQMS, ERP and spreadsheets. Release cycle time carries days of pure document handling, and every excursion or deviation multiplies it. The queue is measurable in release-to-ship lag per batch.
Serialization and cold-chain blind spots

Excursion decisions run on spreadsheets and email chains; traceability between EPCIS events, shipment telemetry and quality dispositions lives in three systems nobody joins. Temperature excursions that should be routine dispositions become investigation events, and DSCSA or FMD audit questions take weeks to answer.
Validation debt stalling every change

Every change to a GxP system triggers a validation cycle sized by checkbox tradition rather than by risk. CSA exists as guidance but not as practice, so the estate fossilizes: the system that cannot change cheaply is the system that gets worked around, and the workarounds become the audit finding.

blocks.x: The pattern across all eight leaks: acceleration is capped by evidence, not by science. ALCOA+ data integrity, replay and reproducibility are engineering properties a system either has or does not — which is why Dataq Software ships every pharma build with its validation pack and provenance layer from the first slice, not at project close.
How Dataq Software works pharmaceuticals and biotech

Dataq Software builds inside the validated estate you already run. We do not arrive with a platform replacement, a rip-and-replace QMS story, or a strategy deck that ends where the hard part begins. The engagement model is engineering-first: a two-week diagnostic that baselines one workflow end to end — eligibility, monitoring, PV intake, release, RWE — then a scoped build that ships behind your change control, behind your CSV/CSA process, and behind the GxP duties that attach to everything the system touches.

Three engineering commitments shape everything we deliver in this sub-industry. First, every automated decision carries replay: inputs, versions, criteria and outcomes are stored so that an inspection, audit or signal question twelve months later is a query, not an investigation. Second, every generative component is permission-aware and citation-bound — safety narratives cite the case record, eligibility rationales cite the source data, and nothing generates free text into a regulated record without a human author of record. Third, every build lands with its validation pack: CSA-aligned risk assessments, test evidence and traceability generated by the build process itself.

The published record behind this approach includes a European biopharma group that matched trial eligibility at 10x and met enrollment windows manual chart review had been missing. The commercial model follows the measurement logic: where the metric is clean — case cycle time, match throughput, release lag — we contract against the delta with the baseline locked during the diagnostic; where it is confounded, we say so in the feasibility read and scope fixed-fee instead.
The builds: six deep engineering services for pharma and biotech

The catalog below is the whole of our pharma and biotech practice. Each build is named for the workflow it changes, sized in the diagnostic, and shipped with the controls the workflow's regulator will expect. None of them require replacing the EDC, the safety database or the QMS; all of them require taking the validation and data-integrity duties seriously.
1. Trial eligibility and recruitment intelligence

The build translates protocol eligibility criteria into computable queries with explicit value sets — OMOP-mapped where your data partners support it, custom mappings documented where they do not — and runs them against EHR-derived and data-partner populations. Every match returns with its evidence: the labs, medications, diagnoses and notes that qualified the patient, so a coordinator confirms in minutes what chart review took hours to find. Site-level telemetry shows where screening converts and where it stalls, so protocol amendments argue from data.

The governance side is built for the regulated context: query definitions are versioned artifacts with lineage, every match decision is replayable, and the criteria library is maintained as a managed asset across the portfolio rather than rebuilt per protocol. In the published record, a European biopharma group matched trial eligibility at 10x and met enrollment windows that manual screening had been missing — the same instrumentation this build ships measures that throughput from day one.
2. Risk-based monitoring and central quality surveillance

The build computes KRIs centrally and continuously: enrollment drift against plan, query aging, data-entry lag, protocol-deviation patterns, site-level data anomalies — scored from EDC, CTMS and IRT event streams rather than assembled monthly in spreadsheets. Monitoring recommendations follow the risk: a site whose data profile changed this week gets attention this week, and the rationale for every trip recommendation is stored with its inputs so the monitoring plan survives an inspection question about why resources moved.

Deviation prediction layers on top: the same event streams train models that flag the conditions that historically precede deviations — lagging queries, inconsistent visit windows, supply interruptions — so sites get a support call before the deviation, not an audit finding after it. SDV effort concentrates where verification matters, and the program is measured in deviations found early, SDV hours per study and monitoring cost per enrolled patient, reported from the platform's own telemetry.
3. Pharmacovigilance intake and signal detection

The build attacks the case queue from both ends. Intake: adverse events from sites, call centers, literature and partner transfers land in one pipeline with language handling, duplicate detection and structured triage; case assembly is automated from the source record with MedDRA coding pre-populated for reviewer confirmation. The E2B case assembles with its narrative pre-drafted from the structured record — the reviewer is the author of record, and every fact in the narrative traces to the case file.

Signal detection runs on the cumulative database with periodicity and methods your GVP process defines: disproportionality analysis, case-series assembly for review, and literature surveillance feeding the same evidence store. Every signal decision — evaluate, refine, close — is logged with its inputs for inspection. The program is measured in days-per-case, percentage of cases worked inside their reporting window and signal-review latency, reported from the pipeline rather than reconstructed from case counts at quarter end.
4. Real-world evidence pipelines with submission-grade provenance

The build turns claims and EHR-derived real-world data into analysis-ready assets with the provenance a submission or payer dossier demands: ingestion with source-to-standard mappings documented, cohort definitions as versioned reproducible artifacts, phenotype algorithms with their validation evidence attached, and analysis datasets that follow CDISC conventions so the assembly survives regulatory scrutiny. Lineage is queryable end to end — from source table to result figure — instead of reconstructed from emails when a reviewer asks.

The same pipelines serve the downstream consumers without a per-study rebuild: label expansions, safety reviews, medical-affairs evidence requests, payer dossier updates and publication support all read from the governed cohort layer. Privacy duties — consent, de-identification, data-partner terms — are enforced at the contract layer, so an evidence project starts with data it is allowed to use rather than with a procurement negotiation. The measurable delta is assembly time: months to weeks per study, with reproducibility as the standing guarantee.
5. Manufacturing data spine: batch release, deviations and serialization

The build joins the manufacturing estate into one event fabric: MES batch execution, LIMS results, eQMS deviations and CAPA, ERP materials and serialization EPCIS events normalized to a common contract layer with GMP-appropriate audit trails. Batch disposition assembles itself: results, deviations, excursion handling and training records collate into the release packet while the batch runs, so the QA disposition decision starts from a complete file instead of a document hunt. Cold-chain telemetry joins the same fabric so excursions trigger structured dispositions rather than email threads.

Deviation and CAPA loops close with evidence: quality events route with their telemetry context attached, effectiveness checks read from the same store, and the CAPA metrics an inspector asks for — aging, recurrence, on-time closure — report from the platform continuously. Serialization traceability answers DSCSA and FMD questions as queries across EPCIS events, shipment telemetry and quality dispositions. The program is measured in release cycle time, deviation aging, excursion disposition time and audit-response latency.
6. Validation acceleration and inspection readiness

The build industrializes the compliance paperwork that caps every change: CSA-aligned risk assessments generated from the system's actual behavior and data criticality, test evidence and traceability matrices produced by the build pipeline, and periodic review artifacts assembled from monitoring telemetry instead of by hand. Validation becomes an engineering by-product with a defensible rationale — the risk-based approach regulators have endorsed — rather than a checkbox ceremony that treats every change as equivalent.

Inspection readiness runs on the same evidence layer: audit trails, ALCOA+ attestations, training records and system documentation collate into response packs on demand, and the gaps a mock inspection would find surface as dashboard items rather than as findings. The measurable deltas are validation cycle time per change, inspection-request turnaround and the percentage of evidence generated by the system itself. This build ships with every other build and stands alone for estates that already carry validation debt.

The hot nodes are where the program's differentiation concentrates: terminology binding across MedDRA, CDISC and OMOP vocabularies, and the eligibility matching engine that turns protocol text into evidence-linked queries. Every flow above the core carries integrity checks, so ALCOA+ duties are enforced by construction rather than by documentation.

blocks.x: The data plane: governed research and clinical data

Every decision gap in pharma traces back to a data gap, and most data gaps trace back to the same habit: each function runs its own estate, extracts its own files, and the joins happen in spreadsheets with no lineage. The data plane build inverts the pattern where it matters. Assay results, EDC events, safety cases, CTMS telemetry, manufacturing events and real-world data land through ingestion pipelines into a governed lakehouse in near real time; the source systems keep running exactly as validated, but the decisions above them stop depending on manual joins.

Governance is engineered, not asserted. Every feed carries a schema contract with a named owner, a freshness SLA and integrity checks against the source system's own controls. Terminology binding is enforced at the contract layer — MedDRA for safety, CDISC for submission data, OMOP for real-world cohorts, WHO Drug for medications — so a cohort means the same thing in the clinical meeting and the submission. Consent and data-partner terms travel with the record, and every derivation is a versioned artifact with lineage a reviewer can query.

blocks.x: The decision layer: scores with inspection tails

Pharma operations run on decisions with inspection tails: an eligibility match decides a patient's path into a trial, a monitoring recommendation moves scarce quality resources, a signal disposition shapes the safety narrative, a release decision moves product. The decision layer treats those tails as first-class requirements. Every decision records its inputs, feature values, model versions, criteria and reason codes in a replay store that answers inspection, audit and signal questions as queries. When an inspector asks why, the answer is retrieved, not reconstructed.

Champion/challenger governance is built in rather than bolted on: challengers run on shadow traffic with performance tracked in the registry the quality function owns, promotions happen through the gates your validation and governance process already defines, and rollbacks are rehearsed rather than improvised. The same decision service layer hosts eligibility scoring, KRI computation, signal triage and release-support analytics, so the governance surface is one registry, one replay store, one set of gates — and the validation pack covers one platform instead of every algorithm separately.
The agentic layer: file assembly without judgment authority

The backlog work in pharma — PV case assembly, eligibility pre-screening, monitoring trip preparation, deviation investigation collation, submission readiness checks — follows patterns an agentic workforce can absorb without touching judgment authority. Dataq Software's agent platform runs digital workers with explicit role scopes: the tools they may call, the systems they may read, the actions that require a human checkpoint and the budget of work per run. Every run logs its steps and outputs to the same evidence store the human workflow uses, so an agent's file is auditable exactly like an analyst's.

Where generative agents add leverage — drafting safety narratives from structured case records, summarizing monitoring trip findings, assembling deviation investigation files — the pattern is grounded generation with citation obligations and human authorship of record. Agents never sign cases, never change a coding decision, never modify validated system records; they move the work to the decision point and stop. Capacity is measured in cleared cases per FTE, which is how the functions that sponsor these programs justify them upward.
Controls and evidence: inspection as a query

The regulatory surface of pharma is the densest validation regime in any industry, and it is growing in exactly the directions these builds touch: data integrity, AI governance and inspection efficiency. Dataq Software's answer is the evidence layer — the artifacts an inspector or auditor will ask for are generated continuously by the systems themselves. blocks.x: Integration engineering: the validated estate stays, the contracts change

Pharma estates are validated, audited and change-averse by design, and the fastest way to fail a program is to promise greenfield. Our integration posture is contractual: we define schema contracts with each system owner, land data through governed APIs and validated interfaces, write back through the integration paths your change control already governs, and keep every new component independently deployable behind feature flags. The safety database, the EDC and the MES are not replaced; they are supplied with better context and drained of the decision work they were never good at.

The vendor chain gets the same treatment. Coding assistance, literature surveillance, eligibility and RWE vendors sit behind an abstraction layer with contract tests, so a vendor swap is a configuration change with a migration runbook rather than a re-validation project. Where a legacy interface must stay, the offload pattern applies: the validated interface keeps running while decision surfaces read from the governed stream the offload produces. This is unglamorous work and it is the reason the builds above hold up in production instead of in a pilot.

blocks.x: The team and the operating rhythm

A pharma build team is small and senior: a lead engineer who has run decision systems in validated estates, data engineers who own the ingestion and contract layer, ML engineers who own scoring and evaluation, a controls engineer who owns the evidence and validation layer, and domain leads who have run PV intake, clinical monitoring, batch release or medical writing in production environments. A QA liaison joins for anything touching GxP scope, and agentic-workflow specialists join for the file-assembly builds. The team works to your release calendar and your change-control vocabulary from the first week.

The rhythm is the same at every client: weekly operations review on the workflow's own telemetry, fortnightly gate submissions to change control and QA, quarterly challenger reviews, and an incident practice that treats the decision store and the evidence layer as production-critical systems — because by the second quarter, they are. Escalations go to named engineers, not to a queue.
Failure modes we design against

Pharma programs fail in known ways, and most of the failure modes are organizational rather than mathematical. We name them in the feasibility read and design against them explicitly, because a program that cannot survive its second quarter — or its first inspection — is not worth starting.

items: Pilot purgatory

blocks.x: Questions pharma and biotech leaders ask us

items: Does generative AI survive GxP scrutiny?

Where it is scoped properly, yes: grounded generation with citation obligations, human authorship of record, validation packs and decision replay. What fails inspection is unscoped free text entering regulated records — which is exactly the pattern the platform forbids.
Who is accountable for an agent-assembled case?

The qualified human reviewer remains the author of record for every case, narrative and decision. Agents assemble and propose; humans confirm and sign. Every run is logged, so accountability is traceable end to end rather than asserted in a policy.
Can eligibility work across our data partners?

Yes. The criteria library compiles to the vocabularies your partners support — OMOP where available, documented custom mappings where not — and every match returns its evidence so site coordinators confirm rather than re-screen from scratch.
How does this change our validation burden?

It moves validation from per-system checkbox ceremonies to CSA-aligned risk assessment generated with the build: data criticality drives test depth, monitoring telemetry drives periodic review, and the pack ships with each release instead of trailing it.
Will monitoring reduction withstand an inspection?

The inspection story is the point: KRI telemetry, trip rationales and deviation-prediction records show regulators why resources moved where they did. Risk-based monitoring was always supposed to work this way; the build makes it demonstrable.
Where does RWE become submission-grade?

When lineage, reproducibility and standards compliance are engineered in from ingestion: CDISC-conformant analysis datasets, versioned cohort definitions, validated phenotype algorithms with their evidence attached. The build produces those properties; the review confirms them.
What about data partner contracts and privacy?

Partner terms, consent scope and de-identification rules are enforced at the contract layer with purpose binding visible in the replay store, so evidence projects start with data the organization is contractually allowed to use.
Who owns the build after you leave?

Your teams, with the runbooks, contracts, validation packs, evaluation suites and registry entries transferred as gate conditions during expansion — not as a closing deliverable. Several programs run entirely in-house after the second quarter.
